claim: The fast pyloric rhythm in Cancer borealis has a frequency of approximately 1 Hz.
source: Within the stomatogastric ganglion (STG) of the crab, Cancer borealis, the fast pyloric rhythm (~1 Hz) and the slow gastric mill rhythm (~0.1 Hz) are precisely coordinated at ~11°C such that there is an integer number of pyloric cycles per gastric mill cycle (integer coupling).
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract with specific frequency value.

claim: The slow gastric mill rhythm in Cancer borealis has a frequency of approximately 0.1 Hz.
source: Within the stomatogastric ganglion (STG) of the crab, Cancer borealis, the fast pyloric rhythm (~1 Hz) and the slow gastric mill rhythm (~0.1 Hz) are precisely coordinated at ~11°C such that there is an integer number of pyloric cycles per gastric mill cycle (integer coupling).
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract with specific frequency value.

claim: The pyloric and gastric mill rhythms are precisely coordinated at approximately 11°C such that there is an integer number of pyloric cycles per gastric mill cycle.
source: Within the stomatogastric ganglion (STG) of the crab, Cancer borealis, the fast pyloric rhythm (~1 Hz) and the slow gastric mill rhythm (~0.1 Hz) are precisely coordinated at ~11°C such that there is an integer number of pyloric cycles per gastric mill cycle (integer coupling).
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract describing integer coupling at specific temperature.

claim: Upon increasing temperature from 7°C to 23°C, both the pyloric and gastric mill oscillators showed similar temperature-dependent increases in cycle frequency.
source: Upon increasing temperature from 7°C to 23°C, both oscillators showed similar temperature-dependent increases in cycle frequency, and integer coupling between the circuits was conserved.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Integer coupling between the pyloric and gastric mill circuits is conserved across temperatures from 7°C to 23°C.
source: Upon increasing temperature from 7°C to 23°C, both oscillators showed similar temperature-dependent increases in cycle frequency, and integer coupling between the circuits was conserved.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Coupled oscillatory circuits are ubiquitous in nervous systems.
source: Coupled oscillators are common in nervous systems.
evidence: Stated directly in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Coordination between oscillatory circuits is often necessary for proper function.
source: Although oscillatory circuits may have distinct frequencies and duty cycles, coordination between them is often necessary for proper function (Nadim et al., 1998; Bartos et al., 1999; Colgin, 2011; Gordon, 2011; Jacobson et al., 2013; Rojas-Líbano et al., 2014; Harris and Gordon, 2015; Karalis et al., 2016; Tamura et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Theta frequency circuits coupled to gamma range circuits are thought to drive both sensory and behavioral processing.
source: For example, theta frequency circuits coupled to those in the gamma range are thought to drive both sensory and behavioral processing (Lisman and Buzsáki, 2008; Fujisawa and Buzsáki, 2011; Gordon, 2011; Lisman and Jensen, 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Memory formation may rely on the phase coupling of discrete populations of neurons with distinct frequency bands in the hippocampus.
source: Memory formation may rely on the phase coupling of discrete populations of neurons with distinct frequency bands in the hippocampus (Tass et al., 1998; Lisman, 2005; Montgomery and Buzsáki, 2007; Scheffer-Teixeira and Tort, 2016; Zheng et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work, with speculative language 'may rely'.

claim: Network uncoupling or improper coupling may lead to disease states and circuit malfunction.
source: Network uncoupling or improper coupling may lead to disease states and circuit malfunction (Moran and Hong, 2011; Kirihara et al., 2012; de Hemptinne et al., 2013; Bahramisharif et al., 2016; Salimpour and Anderson, 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work, with speculative language 'may lead'.

claim: The pyloric rhythm is driven by a three-neuron bursting pacemaker kernel composed of the single Anterior Burster (AB) neuron and two Pyloric Dilator (PD) neurons.
source: The pyloric rhythm (~1 Hz) is driven by a three-neuron bursting pacemaker kernel composed of the single Anterior Burster (AB) neuron and two Pyloric Dilator (PD) neurons (Nadim et al., 1998; Marder and Bucher, 2007).
evidence: Stated directly with citations to prior work.

claim: The gastric mill rhythm is produced by activating a half-center oscillator between the Lateral Gastric (LG) motor neuron and Interneuron 1 (Int1).
source: The gastric mill rhythm (~0.1 Hz) is produced by activating a half-center oscillator (reciprocal inhibition that produces alternating bursts of activity) between the Lateral Gastric (LG) motor neuron and Interneuron 1 (Int1), and depends on a complex set of mechanisms including electrical junctions and modulatory input (Coleman and Nusbaum, 1994; Coleman et al., 1995; Bartos and Nusbaum, 1997; Nadim et al., 1998; Bartos et al., 1999; Marder and Bucher, 2007; Stein et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated directly with citations to prior work.

claim: In the New England Atlantic Ocean, where C. borealis is found, intertidal temperatures normally range from 8°C to 24°C during the summer.
source: In the New England Atlantic Ocean, where C. borealis is found, intertidal temperatures normally range from 8°C to 24°C during the summer and 3°C to 18°C in the winter (Stehlik et al., 1991).
evidence: Stated directly with citation to prior work.

claim: In the New England Atlantic Ocean, where C. borealis is found, intertidal temperatures normally range from 3°C to 18°C in the winter.
source: In the New England Atlantic Ocean, where C. borealis is found, intertidal temperatures normally range from 8°C to 24°C during the summer and 3°C to 18°C in the winter (Stehlik et al., 1991).
evidence: Stated directly with citation to prior work.

claim: The timescales of activation and inactivation of ion channels can change approximately 2 to 20 fold across 10°C.
source: For example, the timescales of activation and inactivation of ion channels can change ~2 to 20 fold across 10°C (Q10s; Zečević et al., 1985; Klöckner et al., 1990; Moran et al., 2004; Cao and Oertel, 2005; Fohlmeister et al., 2010; Tang et al., 2010; Kang et al., 2012; Robertson and Money, 2012; Yang and Zheng, 2014).
evidence: Stated directly with citations to prior work.

claim: The phase relationships between different pyloric neurons are stable between 7°C and 23°C.
source: Although the phase relationships between different pyloric neurons are stable between 7°C and 23°C (Tang et al., 2010; Haddad and Marder, 2018), little is known about temperature compensation in the gastric mill oscillator (Städele et al., 2015) or how temperature affects coupling between the pyloric and gastric mill rhythms.
evidence: Stated directly with citations to prior work.

claim: A key feature of temperature compensation in the pyloric circuit is that the pacemaker kernel of the pyloric rhythm maintains constant duty cycle across a range of temperatures.
source: A key feature of temperature compensation in the pyloric circuit is that the pacemaker kernel of the pyloric rhythm maintains constant duty cycle across a range of temperatures (Tang et al., 2010; Rinberg et al., 2013), and this facilitates temperature compensation of neuron phase relationships in the rest of the circuit.
evidence: Stated directly with citations to prior work.

claim: The pyloric rhythm is constitutively active, with a characteristic period of about 1 s.
source: The pyloric rhythm is constitutively active, with a characteristic period of about 1 s.
evidence: Stated directly in the Results section.

claim: The gastric mill rhythm has a characteristic period of 6 to 10 s.
source: The gastric mill rhythm can be evoked by stimulating projection neurons found within the commissural ganglia (CoGs) and has a characteristic period of 6 to 10 s (Beenhakker et al., 2004).
evidence: Stated directly with citation to prior work.

claim: MCN1 and CPN2 evoke a gastric mill rhythm when stimulated or when they are spontaneously active.
source: The modulatory commissural neuron 1 (MCN1) and commissural projection neuron 2 (CPN2; Figure 1a) evoke a gastric mill rhythm when stimulated or when they are spontaneously active (Materials and methods; Beenhakker and Nusbaum, 2004).
evidence: Stated directly with citation to prior work.

claim: Spontaneous gastric mill rhythms were observed at temperatures between 11°C and 30°C.
source: We inspected a dataset of extracellular recordings of dgn and lgn during temperature ramps (Haddad and Marder, 2018) and found spontaneous gastric mill activity at temperatures between 11°C and 30°C.
evidence: Stated directly as a finding from data analysis.

claim: Spontaneous gastric mill rhythms showed relatively regular activity at lower temperatures but were less regular at higher temperatures.
source: While these recordings show relatively regular gastric mill rhythms at lower temperatures, they were less regular at higher temperatures.
evidence: Stated directly as an observation from the data.

claim: A total of nine preparations showed spontaneous gastric mill rhythms at a variety of different temperatures.
source: Although Figure 2 only shows two examples of spontaneous gastric mill rhythm, there were a total of nine preparations in which spontaneous rhythms were observed at a variety of different temperatures (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated directly with reference to supplemental figure.

claim: Gastric rhythms were evoked across a temperature range of 7 to 21°C in 9 of 10 preparations.
source: We were able to evoke gastric rhythms across a temperature range of 7 to 21°C in 9 of 10 preparations.
evidence: Stated directly as a finding from experiments.

claim: In 4 of 10 preparations, spontaneous gastric mill rhythms were observed at 11°C.
source: In some preparations (4 of 10), spontaneous gastric mill rhythms were observed prior to evoking a rhythm.
evidence: Stated directly as a finding from experiments.

claim: The pyloric cycle period decreases approximately 2-fold with a 10°C increase in temperature.
source: The pyloric cycle period decreases ~2-fold with a 10°C increase in temperature (Tang et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated directly with citation to prior work.

claim: Most preparations (8 of 10) exhibited a cycle period Q10 of approximately 2 for both the pyloric and gastric mill rhythms.
source: Figure 4c shows that most preparations (8 of 10) exhibited a cycle period Q10 of ~2 for both the pyloric and gastric mill rhythms.
evidence: Stated directly as a finding from data analysis.

claim: At 11°C, the gastric mill half-center is capable of producing rhythmic activity even if the pyloric rhythm is turned off by hyperpolarization of the pacemaker neurons.
source: At 11°C, the gastric mill half-center is capable of producing rhythmic activity even if the pyloric rhythm is turned off by hyperpolarization of the pacemaker neurons (Bartos et al., 1999).
evidence: Stated directly with citation to prior work.

claim: In all nine preparations, the gastric mill rhythm was activated at 11°C and 15°C with the pyloric pacemaker both active and inactive.
source: Figure 4—figure supplement 2d shows that in all nine preparations, the gastric mill rhythm was activated at 11°C and 15°C, whereas at 19°C and 21°C only a subset of preparations produced gastric mill rhythms at these elevated temperatures.
evidence: Stated directly with reference to supplemental figure.

claim: At 19°C and 21°C only a subset of preparations produced gastric mill rhythms with the pyloric pacemaker inactive.
source: Figure 4—figure supplement 2d shows that in all nine preparations, the gastric mill rhythm was activated at 11°C and 15°C, whereas at 19°C and 21°C only a subset of preparations produced gastric mill rhythms at these elevated temperatures.
evidence: Stated directly with reference to supplemental figure.

claim: Integer coupling exists between the pyloric and gastric mill oscillators at 11°C.
source: Integer coupling exists between the pyloric and gastric mill oscillators at 11°C (Bartos et al., 1999; Hamood and Marder, 2015).
evidence: Stated directly with citations to prior work.

claim: LG and PD were significantly integer-coupled at temperatures from 7°C to 21°C.
source: LG and PD were significantly integer-coupled, at temperatures from 7°C to 21°C (p < 10–5, D > 0.24), while DG and PD were not significantly coupled at any temperature (p > 0.02, D < 0.16).
evidence: Stated directly with statistical test results.

claim: DG and PD were not significantly coupled at any temperature.
source: LG and PD were significantly integer-coupled, at temperatures from 7°C to 21°C (p < 10–5, D > 0.24), while DG and PD were not significantly coupled at any temperature (p > 0.02, D < 0.16).
evidence: Stated directly with statistical test results.

claim: LG bursts started at a phase of approximately 0.5 in the PD cycle from 7°C to 21°C.
source: From 7°C to 21°C, LG bursts started at a phase of ~0.5 in the PD cycle (Figure 6b, inset), and this phase offset did not significantly trend across this temperature range (p = 0.46, ρ = –0.31, Spearman test).
evidence: Stated directly with statistical test results and reference to figure.

claim: The phase offset between LG burst starts and PD phase did not significantly trend across the temperature range from 7°C to 21°C.
source: From 7°C to 21°C, LG bursts started at a phase of ~0.5 in the PD cycle (Figure 6b, inset), and this phase offset did not significantly trend across this temperature range (p = 0.46, ρ = –0.31, Spearman test).
evidence: Stated directly with statistical test results.

claim: LG burst start probabilities were significantly different from a uniform distribution.
source: LG burst start probabilities were sharply peaked (Figure 6b) and were significantly different from a uniform distribution (Figure 6b, dashed line, p < 4×10–4, 7.5<z<45, Rayleigh test for non-uniformity; see Methods for details).
evidence: Stated directly with statistical test results and reference to figure.

claim: DG burst starts are not always significantly non-uniformly distributed in PD phase.
source: DG burst starts are not always significantly non-uniformly distributed, and the effect size is much smaller (p ∈ [0.001, 0.85], 0.15 < z < 13, Rayleigh test).
evidence: Stated directly with statistical test results and reference to figure.

claim: There is a pronounced decrease in the probability of spiking in LG at higher temperatures close to PD burst termination.
source: We measured the spike probability of LG conditional on PD phase across this temperature range and found a pronounced decrease in the probability of spiking in LG at higher temperatures (Figure 6c). This decrease in LG spike probability occurred close to PD burst termination (Figure 6c, horizontal bars).
evidence: Stated directly with reference to figure.

claim: DG spike probability does not show a noticeable decrease close to the end of PD bursting.
source: DG spike probability also does not show a noticeable decrease close to the end of PD bursting (Figure 6f, Figure 6c).
evidence: Stated directly with reference to figure.

claim: Temperature is a global perturbation that influences the properties of all ion channels and synapses in neuronal circuits.
source: Temperature is a global perturbation that influences the properties of all ion channels and synapses in neuronal circuits (Zečević et al., 1985; Janssen, 1992; Xu and Robertson, 1996; Garrity et al., 2010; Tang et al., 2010; Kang et al., 2012; Robertson and Money, 2012; Marder et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated directly with citations to prior work.

claim: The cardiac ganglion in the crab is temperature-sensitive across a range of physiological temperature with a Q10 of approximately 2.
source: The cardiac ganglion, another circuit in the crab, which governs heartbeat, is also temperature-sensitive across a range of physiological temperature, again with a Q10 of ~2 (Kushinsky et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated directly with citation to prior work.

claim: Coupling between the gastric mill and pyloric circuits is likely to be important for the crab.
source: Coupling of the gastric mill and pyloric circuits is likely to be important for the crab.
evidence: Stated directly with speculative language 'likely to be'.

claim: In the intact animal, muscle movements of the gastric mill enable ingested food to be chewed and subsequently filtered and pumped into the hindgut by the pylorus.
source: In the intact animal, muscle movements of the gastric mill enable ingested food to be chewed and subsequently filtered and pumped into the hindgut by the pylorus (Marder and Bucher, 2007).
evidence: Stated directly with citation to prior work.

claim: Coupling between the pyloric and gastric mill circuits coordinates the timing of chewing and filtering enabling proper flow of food through the mid-gut.
source: Coupling between these circuits coordinates the timing of chewing and filtering enabling proper flow of food through the mid-gut (Meyrand et al., 1994; Diehl et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated directly with citations to prior work.

claim: The pyloric rhythm is temperature-robust because the AB neuron maintains a relatively constant duty cycle across the temperature range.
source: The pyloric rhythm is temperature-robust because the AB neuron maintains a relatively constant duty cycle across this range (Tang et al., 2010; Rinberg et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated directly with citations to prior work.

claim: Temperature robustness in the gastric mill rhythm arises from a different set of interdependent processes including projection neuron input, coordination of the half-center oscillator neurons LG and Int1, and feedback from LG to MCN1.
source: Temperature robustness in the gastric mill rhythm arises from a different set of interdependent processes including projection neuron input, coordination of the half-center oscillator neurons LG and Int1, and feedback from LG to MCN1.
evidence: Stated directly as an inference from the findings.

claim: The similarity between the apparent cycle period Q10s of the pyloric and gastric mill rhythms was unexpected.
source: The similarity between the apparent cycle period Q10s of the pyloric and gastric mill rhythms was unexpected as there are so many different physiological processes generating the two rhythms.
evidence: Stated directly as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: There are at least 10 known processes of gastric mill rhythm generation.
source: There are 10 known processes of gastric mill rhythm generation and all but two produce distinct motor patterns from one another (Heinzel et al., 1993; Coleman and Nusbaum, 1994; Norris et al., 1994; Norris et al., 1996; Weimann et al., 1997; Blitz et al., 1999; Christie et al., 2004; Saideman et al., 2007a; Saideman et al., 2007b; White and Nusbaum, 2011; Dickinson et al., 2015; Blitz et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated directly with citations to prior work.

claim: All but two of the 10 known gastric mill rhythm generation processes produce distinct motor patterns from one another.
source: There are 10 known processes of gastric mill rhythm generation and all but two produce distinct motor patterns from one another (Heinzel et al., 1993; Coleman and Nusbaum, 1994; Norris et al., 1994; Norris et al., 1996; Weimann et al., 1997; Blitz et al., 1999; Christie et al., 2004; Saideman et al., 2007a; Saideman et al., 2007b; White and Nusbaum, 2011; Dickinson et al., 2015; Blitz et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated directly with citations to prior work.

claim: One gastric mill rhythm variant is easily disrupted by small temperature changes.
source: A previous study showed that one gastric mill rhythm variant is easily disrupted by small temperature changes (Städele et al., 2015), while the one studied here maintains rhythmicity following a large increase in temperature.
evidence: Stated directly with citation to prior work.

claim: Neuromodulatory substances can extend the temperature range over which the gastric and pyloric rhythms maintain function.
source: Previous work has shown that neuromodulatory substances can extend the temperature range over which the gastric and pyloric rhythms maintain function (Städele et al., 2015; Haddad and Marder, 2018).
evidence: Stated directly with citations to prior work.

claim: In C. elegans neuromodulation enhances the robustness of thermosensory neurons and altering temperature-dependent behavior.
source: In C. elegans neuromodulation enhances the robustness of thermosensory neurons and altering temperature-dependent behavior (Beverly et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated directly with citation to prior work.

claim: In crayfish, the rectifying electrical junction from the lateral giant fiber to the motor giant fiber has reliable synaptic propagation between 20°C and 30°C.
source: In crayfish, the rectifying electrical junction from the lateral giant fiber to the motor giant fiber has reliable synaptic propagation between 20°C and 30°C (Heitler and Edwards, 1998).
evidence: Stated directly with citation to prior work.

claim: Input resistance modestly decreases in both the Lateral Pyloric (LP) and LG neurons with increased temperature.
source: Previous work showed that input resistance modestly decreases in both the Lateral Pyloric (LP) and LG neurons with increased temperature (Tang et al., 2010; Städele et al., 2015).
evidence: Stated directly with citations to prior work.

claim: In the pyloric circuit, the IPSP amplitude in the LP neuron is temperature-invariant (Q10 approximately 1).
source: In the pyloric circuit, the IPSP amplitude in the LP neuron is temperature-invariant (Q10 ~1), but the IPSC amplitude increased (Q10 ~2.5) across the same range of temperatures as those studied here (Tang et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated directly with citation to prior work.

claim: In the pyloric circuit, the IPSC amplitude in the LP neuron increased with temperature (Q10 approximately 2.5).
source: In the pyloric circuit, the IPSP amplitude in the LP neuron is temperature-invariant (Q10 ~1), but the IPSC amplitude increased (Q10 ~2.5) across the same range of temperatures as those studied here (Tang et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated directly with citation to prior work.

claim: Both IA and Ih currents exhibit temperature-dependent increases in activation rate and peak current (Q10s approximately 2 to 4).
source: Both IA and Ih (currents that promote bursting and PIR) exhibit temperature-dependent increases in activation rate and peak current (Q10s ~ 2 to 4; Tang et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated directly with citation to prior work.

claim: The nervous systems of small homeotherms such as birds, rodents and human infants likely face similar challenges as a result of fluctuations in ambient temperature or in fever response to illness.
source: The nervous systems of small homeotherms such as birds, rodents (Chaffee and Roberts, 1971; Janssen, 1992) and even human infants (Mank et al., 2016; Barbi et al., 2017) likely face similar challenges as a result of fluctuations in ambient temperature or in fever response to illness.
evidence: Stated directly with citations and speculative language 'likely face'.

claim: The pyloric oscillator is robust to large changes in pH.
source: For example, the pyloric oscillator is known to be robust to large changes in pH (Haley et al., 2018) and to fluctuations in extracellular potassium (He et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated directly with citation to prior work.

claim: The pyloric oscillator is robust to fluctuations in extracellular potassium.
source: For example, the pyloric oscillator is known to be robust to large changes in pH (Haley et al., 2018) and to fluctuations in extracellular potassium (He et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated directly with citation to prior work.

claim: Adult male Jonah crabs (C. borealis) were kept in tanks with circulating artificial sea water at 11°C for approximately 1 week prior to use.
source: Adult male Jonah crabs (C. borealis; N = 19 from Commercial Lobster [Boston, MA] and N = 9 from Moody's Seafood [Brunswick, ME]) were kept in tanks with circulating artificial sea water at 11°C for approximately 1 week prior to use.
evidence: Stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Preparations with spontaneous rhythms (N = 9) were from crabs caught in July 2013.
source: Preparations with spontaneous rhythms (N = 9) were from crabs caught in July 2013 and studied soon thereafter.
evidence: Stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Preparations in which rhythms were evoked (N = 10) were from crabs caught in July, September, and December of 2017.
source: Preparations in which rhythms were evoked (N = 10) were from crabs caught in July, September, and December of 2017.
evidence: Stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Preparations in which the pyloric pacemaker was inhibited (N = 9) were from crabs caught in August and September 2020.
source: Preparations in which the pyloric pacemaker was inhibited (N = 9) were from crabs caught in August and September 2020.
evidence: Stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The dorsal posterior esophageal nerves (dpons) were bilaterally stimulated to elicit a gastric mill rhythm.
source: We bilaterally stimulated the dorsal posterior esophageal nerves (dpons) to elicit a gastric mill rhythm (Figure 1a, b).
evidence: Stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Ten, six-second long episodic stimulus trains (0.6 Hz) were used to evoke gastric mill rhythms using a within-train stimulus rate of 15 Hz.
source: Ten, six-second long episodic stimulus trains (0.6 Hz) were used to evoke gastric mill rhythms using a within-train stimulus rate of 15 Hz, as described in Beenhakker and Nusbaum, 2004.
evidence: Stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The dpons contain axons of the ventral cardiac neurons (VCNs) that activate the MCN1 and CPN2.
source: The dpons contain axons of the ventral cardiac neurons (VCNs) that activate the MCN1 and CPN2, resulting in a VCN-gastric mill rhythm that is often active for tens of minutes (Beenhakker et al., 2004; Beenhakker and Nusbaum, 2004; Blitz and Nusbaum, 2008).
evidence: Stated directly with citations to prior work.

claim: VCN stimulation results in a VCN-gastric mill rhythm that is often active for tens of minutes.
source: The dpons contain axons of the ventral cardiac neurons (VCNs) that activate the MCN1 and CPN2, resulting in a VCN-gastric mill rhythm that is often active for tens of minutes (Beenhakker et al., 2004; Beenhakker and Nusbaum, 2004; Blitz and Nusbaum, 2008).
evidence: Stated directly with citations to prior work.

claim: The VCN-gastric mill rhythms were difficult to generate consistently above 23°C.
source: The VCN-gastric mill rhythms were difficult to generate consistently above 23°C, and in some cases only persisted for several cycles.
evidence: Stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Within the temperature range in which they were readily evoked, gastric mill rhythms lasted for tens of minutes.
source: Within the temperature range in which they were readily evoked, gastric mill rhythms lasted for tens of minutes.
evidence: Stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The accuracy of spike classification using the neural network always exceeded 98%.
source: The accuracy of the classification was constantly monitored during sorting, and new annotations were used to continuously re-train the network using an active learning framework. Classification accuracy always exceeded 98%.
evidence: Stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Bursts in PD, LG, or DG were defined using inter-spike intervals (ISIs) longer than 1 second.
source: Bursts in PD, LG, or DG were defined using inter-spike intervals (ISIs). ISIs longer than 1 second on LG or DG were defined to be an inter-burst interval and were used to annotate the start of a burst.
evidence: Stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: A total of n = 3816 LG burst starts and n = 3228 DG burst starts across nine temperature points and 10 preparations are plotted in Figure 6b,d.
source: A total of n = 3816 LG burst starts and n = 3228 DG burst starts across nine temperature points and 10 preparations are plotted in Figure 6b,d.
evidence: Stated directly in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The AB and PD neurons are strongly electrically coupled.
source: Because the AB and PD neurons are strongly electrically coupled, the cycle period of the pyloric pacemaker can be monitored using the pdn (Figure 1b), which contains only PD neuron action potentials.
evidence: Stated directly in the Results section.

claim: MCN1 excites all neurons in the STG, including the pyloric pacemaker and gastric mill half-center neurons (LG and Int1).
source: While CPN2 drives the gastric mill circuit via electrical synapses onto key motor neurons (LG and GM), MCN1 excites all neurons in the STG, including the pyloric pacemaker and gastric mill half-center neurons (LG and Int1; Figure 1d).
evidence: Stated directly with reference to figure.

claim: CPN2 drives the gastric mill circuit via electrical synapses onto key motor neurons (LG and GM).
source: While CPN2 drives the gastric mill circuit via electrical synapses onto key motor neurons (LG and GM), MCN1 excites all neurons in the STG, including the pyloric pacemaker and gastric mill half-center neurons (LG and Int1; Figure 1d).
evidence: Stated directly with reference to figure.

claim: Both pattern-generating circuits provide feedback to MCN1 and CPN2 projection neurons.
source: Both pattern-generating circuits provide feedback to these projection neurons (Norris et al., 1994; Blitz and Nusbaum, 2008; Blitz and Nusbaum, 2012; Blitz, 2017).
evidence: Stated directly with citations to prior work.

claim: Rhythmic AB inhibition of Int1 results in LG disinhibition and firing following the peak of Int1 inhibition.
source: The cartoon voltage traces (Figure 1d) demonstrate integer coupling between the pyloric and gastric mill circuits, where rhythmic AB inhibition of Int1 results in LG disinhibition and firing following the peak of Int1 inhibition (Nadim et al., 1998; Bartos et al., 1999).
evidence: Stated directly with citations to prior work and reference to figure.

claim: The salient drivers of LG firing are sufficient projection neuron excitation and disinhibition from Int1.
source: Because the salient drivers of LG firing are sufficient projection neuron excitation and disinhibition from Int1 (Bartos et al., 1999; DeLong et al., 2009), the total number of pyloric cycles per gastric mill cycle can vary greatly.
evidence: Stated directly with citations to prior work.

claim: Modulation of LG spiking by AB/PD has been reported via feedback from AB to MCN1 and CPN2.
source: Modulation of LG spiking by AB/PD has been reported via feedback from AB to MCN1 and CPN2 (Blitz and Nusbaum, 2008) and possibly Int1 feedback to CPN2 (Blitz, 2017).
evidence: Stated directly with citations to prior work.

claim: DG is not directly coupled to the pyloric oscillator.
source: Although DG bursts on the same timescale as LG, it is not directly coupled to the pyloric oscillator (Figure 1) and does not show any signature of phase coupling with PD.
evidence: Stated directly with reference to figure.

claim: If LG bursts start at a particular phase in the PD cycle, then the burst periods of LG and PD must be integer-coupled.
source: If LG bursts start at a particular phase in the PD cycle, then the burst periods of LG and PD must be integer-coupled (Nadim et al., 1998).
evidence: Stated directly with citation to prior work.
